reason: The sources robustly corroborate dozens of facts about Saturn's periodic Great White Spot megastorms across multiple independent sites.
story: Every 20 to 30 years—roughly once a Saturnian year—Saturn unleashes a colossal megastorm known as a Great White Spot. First cataloged in 1876, six of these planetary tempests have erupted over the past 140 years, alternating between the equator and mid-latitudes. When a storm erupts, a thunderous head as wide as planet Earth generates up to ten lightning strikes per second. High-altitude winds whip the storm into a turbulent tail that stretches tens of thousands of kilometers around the gas giant until it literally collides with its own head, completely encircling the planet. Planetary scientists discovered that the storms are bottled up for decades because heavy water vapor precipitates out and suppresses atmospheric convection until the cooling upper layers catastrophically destabilize. Long after the clouds vanish, radio observations reveal that chemical scars from these colossal upheavals linger inside Saturn's atmosphere for centuries.
angle: Saturn periodically generates an Earth-sized thunderstorm so immense that its tail wraps completely around the 235,000-mile planet until it crashes into its own head.

claims.claim: Great White Spots are massive planet-encircling storms that periodically erupt on Saturn.
Six Great White Spot megastorms have been documented on Saturn since 1876.
The storms erupt roughly every 20 to 30 years, approximately once every Saturnian year.
The storms are named 'Great White Spots' by analogy to Jupiter's Great Red Spot.
Great White Spots alternate between Saturn's equatorial region and its mid-latitudes.
The storms typically emerge when Saturn's northern hemisphere is tilted most toward the Sun.
The head of a Great White Spot can grow to a size comparable to Earth.
The storm head develops a massive tail that wraps entirely around the planet until it catches up with itself.
The most recent Great White Spot emerged in late 2010.
The 2010 storm was observed up close by NASA's Cassini spacecraft.
The 2010 storm grew to encircle the entire planet within six months.
The 2010 storm generated an intense lightning rate of up to 10 electrostatic discharge flashes per second.
Caltech scientists Andrew Ingersoll and Cheng Li proposed that water vapor suppresses atmospheric convection to cause the multi-decade delay between storms.
Water molecules are heavy compared to hydrogen and helium, sinking and leaving the upper atmosphere less dense until cooling overrides the suppression.
Jupiter is thought to lack planet-encircling storms because its upper atmosphere contains less water vapor than Saturn's.
Atmospheric anomalies and chemical remnants of Great White Spots persist in Saturn's atmosphere for centuries after the visible storms dissipate.
The Cassini mission ended in September 2017 when the spacecraft plunged into Saturn's atmosphere.

disputed: Whether the 2010 storm was early: S1 notes it occurred 'ahead of its time shortly after equinox' and S7 notes it was 'a decade earlier than expected', whereas S4 and S5 describe it as fitting the regular 20 to 30 year cadence (occurring 20 years after the 1990 storm); scripts should attribute specific forecasting expectations rather than stating it was universally considered premature.
